title: A Fully Human Monoclonal Antibody Cocktail Provides Therapeutic Protection Against Botulinum Neurotoxin A1.
abstract: Botulism is a fatal disease characterized by flaccid paralysis caused by botulinum neurotoxin (BoNT). In adults, human botulism is currently treated with equine-derived antitoxins, which have provided substantial clinical benefit and remain the mainstay of treatment. However, these equine antitoxin products carry a risk of adverse reactions due to heterologous proteins and have limitations in stable supply. Here, we developed three fully human monoclonal antibodies (HuMAbs)-BT-015, BT-175, and NT-320-against botulinum neurotoxin subtype A1 (BoNT/A1), a major cause of human botulism. BT-015 and BT-175 bound to recombinant LHN, which comprises the catalytic domain (light chain) and the N-terminal translocation domain of the heavy chain, whereas NT-320 bound to the C-terminal receptor-binding domain of the heavy chain (HC). Competition assays further showed that BT-015 and BT-175 recognize largely distinct binding sites within LHN. Each antibody showed neutralizing activity in mice, whereas the three-antibody cocktail provided the greatest protective effect and completely protected mice against the BoNT/A1 medium progenitor toxin complex (M-PTC) under the conditions tested. Moreover, treatment with the cocktail shortly after the onset of clinical signs following oral challenge with the BoNT/A1 large progenitor toxin complex (L-PTC) improved survival and promoted recovery from clinical signs. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of the HuMAb cocktail for botulism.

title: Recombinant Oligoclonal Antibody Botulinum Antitoxins Are a Low-Cost Alternative to Equine Antitoxin.
abstract: We have developed highly potent botulinum neurotoxin (BoNT) antitoxins consisting of three mAbs that bind non-overlapping epitopes and act synergistically to neutralize and rapidly clear circulating toxin. The resulting potency permits a low total antibody dose for treatment (34 mg for a seven-serotype product under the assumptions used here). Based on this high potency, the cost of producing the drug substance per dose is relatively low relative to chronic, high-dose antibody therapeutics. Recombinant human IgG also provides a longer serum half-life than equine F(ab')2 antitoxin and therefore has potential for both treatment and prevention of botulism lasting for months. Here, we analyze the manufacturing costs of the recombinant antitoxin and the development costs of multivalent products and compare them to those of the currently approved equine-derived antitoxin. Approaches to reducing manufacturing complexity, including co-expression and co-purification, formulation, stockpiling, clinical use, analytical control, and multivalent antibody formats, are discussed. Our analysis indicates that recombinant oligoclonal BoNT antitoxins are not intrinsically cost-prohibitive and that development and overall manufacturing costs of Drug Product do not increase linearly with the number of serotypes covered.

title: Polystyrene Nanoplastics and Lead Co-Exposure: A Hypothesis-Driven Framework for Trophoblast Injury at the Maternal-Fetal Interface.
abstract: Micro- and nanoplastics can coexist with lead (Pb) in environmental media, raising the possibility of maternal co-exposure during pregnancy. Polystyrene nanoplastics (PS-NPs), owing to their high specific surface area, can adsorb Pb2+, potentially altering its bioavailability and tissue distribution through a proposed Trojan horse effect. This narrative review integrates evidence from placental, reproductive, and nonplacental models to explore the potential effects of PS-NPs and Pb co-exposure on placental trophoblast cells. Based on the available evidence, we propose a trophoblast-centered, testable framework in which PS-NPs and Pb, whether transiently associated or arriving through separate pathways, may converge at the maternal-fetal interface, promote oxidative stress, disrupt endoplasmic reticulum homeostasis, and shift unfolded protein response signaling toward apoptosis. By linking potential co-exposure pathways with trophoblast stress responses, this framework provides experimentally tractable directions for reproductive toxicology. Direct evidence demonstrating that Pb remains associated with PS-NPs during maternal circulation or within the placenta is limited; thus, the proposed framework should be regarded as a testable hypothesis rather than an established mechanism. Future studies should prioritize environmentally relevant exposure levels, factorial co-exposure designs, particle-specific tracking, and human-relevant trophoblast or placental models to define mixture interactions and establish causal relationships within the proposed pathway.

title: Micro- and Nanoplastics as Emerging Cardiovascular Stressors: Mechanisms of Vascular Injury, Atherothrombosis, and Myocardial Dysfunction.
journal: Journal of cardiovascular development and disease
abstract: Micro- and nanoplastics (MNPs) are gaining prominence as human-made pollutants that continuously enter the human body through ingestion, inhalation, and iatrogenic routes. Current analytical technologies utilizing vibrational chemical imaging and thermal degradation mass spectrometry have established that these materials enter blood circulation and accumulate in the human cardiovascular system (blood, arteries, plaques, thrombi, and myocardium). MNPs function as a unique combination of solid and chemical pollutants since the materials contain an insoluble polymer core, formulation-specific additives, such as phthalates and bisphenols that can leach into the surrounding milieu, and contaminants that adsorb to the surface. This phenomenon, called the "Trojan horse" effect, explains this property of MNPs. Experimental studies have demonstrated their ability to degrade the endothelial glycocalyx and uncouple endothelial nitric oxide synthase. MNPs also trigger mitochondrial stress, which activates the NLRP3 inflammasome pathway. These mechanisms can contribute to multiple cardiovascular diseases like atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), acute coronary syndromes (ACS), heart failure, arrhythmia, and thromboembolism. The findings from human surgical cohorts show that there is a connection between polymer accumulation in plaques, the development of vascular inflammation, the structural vulnerability of plaques, and the incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events. However, it is important to understand that these results are not sufficient for establishing definitive clinical causality. Most human data come from cross-sectional studies that can suffer from reverse causation, such as when inflamed, hyperpermeable vascular walls allow the entrance of the pollutants without them being the direct cause of the disease. To reach a definite conclusion about the connection between MNPs and cardiovascular diseases, it is essential to conduct intervention studies and establish prospective longitudinal exposure cohorts.

title: Genetic diversity and population structure of native and translocated Bashkir horse (Equus ferus caballus) populations based on microsatellite markers.
abstract: The Bashkir horse (Equus ferus caballus) is an indigenous Russian breed with a unique adaptive gene pool that is important for biodiversity conservation and sustainable breeding. However, information on the genetic differentiation between native and recently translocated populations remains limited. This study evaluated the genetic diversity, population structure, and within-breed differentiation of native Bashkir horses from the Republic of Bashkortostan and a translocated population established in the Tver Region using microsatellite markers. A total of 240 Bashkir horses were included, comprising a native population from the Republic of Bashkortostan (n = 190) and a translocated population from the Tver Region (n = 50). Genomic DNA extracted from hair follicles was genotyped at 17 International Society for Animal Genetics (ISAG)-recommended microsatellite loci using the COrDIS Horse kit. Genetic diversity indices, including the number of alleles, effective number of alleles, Shannon index, observed and expected heterozygosity, polymorphic information content (PIC), and Wright's fixation indices, were calculated. Population differentiation was evaluated using principal coordinates analysis (PCoA), pairwise fixation index among subpopulations (FST), permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA), and Bayesian clustering with STRUCTURE and the Evanno method. Analysis of the 17 microsatellite loci identified 160 alleles in the native population and 137 alleles in the translocated population, with mean allele numbers of 9.41 and 8.06 per locus, respectively. The loci ASB17, ASB2, and HTG10 contributed most to genetic diversity in both populations. Mean effective allele numbers were 4.783 and 4.713, whereas the Shannon index averaged 1.741 and 1.676 for the native and translocated populations, respectively. High PIC values confirmed the excellent discriminatory power of the marker panel. Low mean inbreeding coefficient within subpopulations (0.012) and overall inbreeding coefficient (0.022) values indicated minimal inbreeding. PERMANOVA detected statistically significant but extremely weak population differentiation (F = 3.28, R² = 0.0136, p = 0,001, whereas bootstrapped FST (0.0072 ± 0.0012; 95% confidence interval: 0.0045-0.0093) demonstrated very low genetic divergence. Bayesian clustering identified K = 3 as the optimal model, revealing subdivision within the native Bashkir population while preserving the overall genetic integrity of the breed. Native and translocated Bashkir horse populations have retained high genetic diversity and exhibit only minimal genetic differentiation despite approximately two decades of geographic separation. The combined use of microsatellite markers with complementary population genetic analyses provides robust evidence supporting the conservation of the Bashkir horse gene pool while identifying subtle within-breed substructure. These findings provide a scientific foundation for genetic monitoring, conservation planning, pedigree management, and sustainable breeding programs for this valuable indigenous horse breed.

title: Left ventricular mass and allometrically scaled dimensions in athletic Quarter Horses: Preliminary echocardiographic reference values for Vaquejada athletes.
abstract: Echocardiographic data for Quarter Horses competing in Vaquejada remain limited. To characterize differences in left ventricular mass (LVM), geometry, and resting systolic indices between athletic and non-trained Quarter Horses and describe preliminary echocardiographic reference values. Fifty Vaquejada athletes and 15 contemporaneous controls underwent echocardiography. LVM was estimated from linear dimensions and indexed to body surface area. Analyses included Welch tests, regression adjusted for age and body weight, and empirical percentiles. Interobserver agreement was assessed in 15 athletes. Athletes were older and heavier. LVM was 3004.64 ± 582.95 versus 1921.13 ± 134.16 g (+56.4%), and indexed LVM was 493.91 ± 92.45 versus 333.23 ± 23.23 g/m² (+48.2%; both P < 0.001). The adjusted LVM difference was +624.43 g (95% confidence interval 398.99-849.87; P < 0.001). Athletes had larger ventricular internal diameters (12.25 versus 9.48 cm), lower relative wall thickness (0.371 versus 0.471), and lower fractional shortening (35.66 versus 41.46%) and ejection fraction (61.97 versus 69.97%; all P < 0.001). Unscaled wall-thickness measures did not differ significantly. The LVM intraclass correlation coefficient was 0.9998. Greater estimated LVM and a distinct ventricular geometric pattern characterized Vaquejada athletes after adjustment for age and weight. Preliminary echocardiographic reference values provide population-specific descriptive data requiring validation. Cross-sectional findings do not establish physiological adaptation or exclude occult disease.

title: Massive mandibular osteolysis associated with a presumptive diagnosis of ameloblastic carcinoma in a horse: clinical, computed tomographic, necropsy, histopathological, and immunohistochemical findings.
abstract: A 15-year-old mixed-breed male horse was presented for evaluation of a firm right mandibular swelling associated with mandibular deviation, trismus, hyporexia, and reduced body condition. Radiography revealed an aggressive osteolytic lesion of the right mandible, but superimposition limited assessment of its anatomical extent. Computed tomography demonstrated an extensive lytic-expansile lesion extending from tooth 406 to the mandibular angle, with cortical disruption, trabecular and medullary replacement, and adjacent soft tissue involvement. Because complete excision with functional mandibular reconstruction was considered unfeasible, euthanasia was elected. Necropsy revealed a poorly demarcated, locally invasive mandibular mass. Histopathology demonstrated a malignant odontogenic epithelial neoplasm with ameloblastic differentiation, destructive bone invasion, high mitotic activity, and a prominent spindle-cell component. Immunohistochemistry confirmed epithelial differentiation through AE1/AE3 and 34βE12 immunoreactivity and demonstrated widespread vimentin expression in the morphologically neoplastic spindle-cell population; SOX10 immunoreactivity was absent. Integration of the histomorphological, immunohistochemical, imaging, and necropsy findings supported the diagnosis of ameloblastic carcinoma with a prominent spindle-cell component and highlighted the value of computed tomography in defining lesion extent and surgical feasibility.

title: Evaluation of the Suture Length-to-Wound Length Ratio as a Risk Factor for Surgical Site Infection after Exploratory Laparotomy in Horses.
abstract: Surgical site infection (SSI) is a common complication of exploratory laparotomy in horses. The suture length-to-wound length (SL:WL) ratio (suture length divided by wound length) indicates closure quality in human surgery, where a ratio of at least 4:1 reduces incisional hernia, but its relevance to SSI in horses is unknown. To determine whether the SL:WL ratio is associated with SSI after exploratory laparotomy in horses. Retrospective study of 76 horses that underwent exploratory laparotomy for colic and survived at least 15 days. SSI was defined as purulent or persistent serous/serosanguineous incisional drainage within 15 days. The SL:WL ratio was analysed as a continuous variable and in four categories (≤5, >5 and <6, ≥6 and <7, ≥7). Variables with univariable likelihood-ratio test P < 0.20 were considered for multivariable logistic regression. Of the 76 horses, 20 (26.3%) developed SSI. The median SL:WL ratio was 5.98 (range 3.26-10.9). The ratio was not associated with SSI in univariable analysis (odds ratio [OR] 1.12 per unit, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.76-1.63) or after adjustment for pyrexia (OR 1.20, 95% CI 0.81-1.78). SSI occurred in 23.1%, 28.0%, 14.3% and 41.2% of horses across the four categories (P = 0.302). Pyrexia before the clinical diagnosis of SSI was associated with SSI (adjusted OR 3.21, 95% CI 1.06-9.66). In these 76 horses, the SL:WL ratio was not associated with SSI, either as a continuous variable or across categories, whereas pyrexia preceding the clinical diagnosis of SSI was.

title: Concurrent ipsilateral mandibular condylectomy, meniscectomy, and partial ceratohyoidectomy in two horses.
abstract: To report concurrent degenerative change of the equine temporomandibular joint (TMJ) and temporohyoid osteoarthropathy (THO) and document the success of ipsilateral mandibular condylectomy, meniscectomy and partial ceratohyoidectomy (IMCPC). Case report. Two client-owned horses presenting to an academic institution hospital. Two horses were diagnosed with severe degenerative TMJ disease and THO. One horse presented with anorexia, pyrexia, and unilateral temporal swelling. Computed tomography (CT) revealed severe left TMJ degeneration, fluid in the left middle ear, and bilateral moderate THO. Left IMCPC was performed. The second case presented 4 months after recovering from strangles with unilateral temporal swelling and masseter and temporalis muscle atrophy. Standing head CT revealed severe left TMJ degeneration and THO along with mild right THO. Left IMCPC was performed. Horse 1 recovered with left-sided facial nerve deficits that improved before discharge on day 10 following surgery. At discharge, the horse was eating alfalfa cubes, hay, and pelleted feed. The owners reported a high level of satisfaction. The horse was euthanized 2 years postoperatively because of severe laminitis unrelated to the surgical procedure. Horse 2 was lost to long-term follow up but was eating alfalfa cubes, hay, and pelleted feed at discharge on day 7. In cases of severe degenerative TMJ disease and THO, IMCPC can be performed to improve clinical signs associated with these conditions. The relationship between THO, TMJ, and inner ear inflammation warrants further investigation, but concurrent disease can be addressed through a single-stage surgical procedure.

title: Environmental Factors Display Multiple Associations with West Nile Virus Risk Modeling in Kansas.
journal: Vector borne and zoonotic diseases (Larchmont, N.Y.)
abstract: West Nile virus (WNV) persists as a significant vector-borne disease in the United States, yet risk prediction frameworks vary widely across the Midwest and often rely on sparse case data or limited mosquito surveillance. These challenges are amplified by the asymptomatic nature of WNV infection. Incorporating publicly available environmental and landscape variables-such as temperature, precipitation, drought indices, and land cover-may offer a more robust and scalable foundation for regional WNV risk assessment. Seven years of human and equine WNV case data were integrated with Culex mosquito surveillance records, county-level land cover, and weekly temperature, precipitation, and drought indices for the state of Kansas. Mosquito abundance from 26 unique trapping sites was assessed using annual regression models, and case occurrence was evaluated using zero-inflated negative binomial models. Site-level trend assessments examined ecological patterns in relation to precipitation, drought, and habitat composition. Lagged temperature and drought severity were the most stable environmental indicators of case occurrence, supported by trend-level contrasts between drought and nondrought seasons. Landscape composition shaped mosquito responses to precipitation and moisture availability. Although Culex abundance showed a significant monotonic association with WNV cases at a 3-week lag, regression models did not detect a linear relationship. Publicly available, routinely updated, and geographically resolved environmental indicators can support a scalable WNV risk assessment framework. This study represents the first integration of these environmental, landscape, and surveillance factors for Kansas and provides a foundation for future work incorporating viral testing of mosquito pools, finer-scale land use data, and more consistent trap placement to strengthen predictive capacity.

title: Effects of equine-assisted services in psychiatric disorders: a systematic review.
abstract: For several years, psychosocial rehabilitation programs have been offered to psychiatric patients as a complement to pharmacological treatment. These programs include Equine-Assisted Services (EAS). Horses are social, highly attentive, and emotionally sensitive animals, making equine-assisted interventions a particularly suitable complementary therapy. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the current state of knowledge regarding the effects of EAS on biopsychosocial outcomes in psychiatry. In accordance with PRISMA guidelines, Embase, EBSCOhost, PubMed, and Web of Science were searched up to February 10, 2026. Only primary research articles in English or French targeting populations with diagnosed psychiatric conditions, involving live horses, and reporting qualitative or quantitative biopsychosocial outcomes were included. Reviews and meta-analyses were excluded. Study quality was evaluated using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool, and data were analyzed using spreadsheets and pivot tables. Out of 888 identified records, 107 articles were included, representing 3,097 participants (65% male). The literature comprised quantitative (40% longitudinal, 17% randomized controlled trials, 12% non-randomized trials), qualitative (22%), and mixed-methods studies (9%), predominantly published by American (49%) or European (35%) teams. Study populations included children/adolescents (55%), adults (24%), and veterans (21%). Interventions primarily targeted neurodevelopmental (43%) and trauma-related disorders (25%). Most programs (78%) combined riding with unmounted activities but lacked standardization in terminology, content, and duration. EAS demonstrated substantial benefits for clinical symptoms, quality of life, and biopsychosocial skills, yielding 99% positive qualitative results and 69% positive quantitative results. The largest improvements occurred in symptom severity, social skills, and motor skills in neurodevelopmental disorders. However, overall methodological quality was low, with widespread biases, small sample sizes, and a frequent lack of control groups or statistical testing. EAS represents a promising and innovative complementary therapy in psychiatry. This review highlights the need for standardized programs and more rigorous research with high levels of evidence (randomized controlled trials) to scientifically validate their effectiveness on clinical symptoms and psychosocial skills. PROSPERO, CRD42021246614. All data generated or analysed during this study are included in this published article.

title: Evaluation of Laboratory Techniques for the Diagnosis of Leptospira-Associated Equine Recurrent Uveitis (ERU) With Focus on the Goldmann-Witmer Coefficient.
Serum homocysteine concentration in apparently healthy thoroughbred geldings.
abstract: Homocysteine (HCY) is a biomarker associated with coagulation, vascular, and neurodegenerative disorders in humans and small animals, but its relevance in equine medicine remains poorly defined. As a central intermediate in one-carbon metabolism, HCY is remethylated to methionine through a folate (FA)-dependent pathway, making FA an important determinant of circulating HCY concentrations. Thyroid hormones may further influence HCY homeostasis through effects on enzymes involved in one-carbon metabolism. Therefore, evaluating HCY in relation to FA and total thyroxine (TT4) may provide insight into factors governing HCY concentrations in horses. This cross-sectional observational study evaluated serum HCY in relation to age, TT4, and FA in trained, apparently healthy Thoroughbred geldings. Eighty-eight horses were recruited; 61 met the inclusion criteria and were classified as apparently healthy, and a subset of 19 with haematological and biochemical results within reference intervals was classified as clinically healthy. In apparently healthy horses, those aged ≥ 10 years had significantly higher HCY (median 8.72 µmol/L) and FA (17.8 nmol/L) and significantly lower TT4 (11.6 nmol/L) than horses aged < 10 years (p = 0.003, p = 0.03, and p = 0.007, respectively); HCY correlated weakly with age (r = 0.29, p = 0.022). In horses aged ≥ 10 years, HCY was moderately positively correlated with TT4 (r = 0.58, p = 0.048). The age-related increase in HCY was also supported in clinically healthy horses (median 5.7 vs. 9.98 µmol/L for < 10 vs. ≥ 10 years; p = 0.046). These findings indicate that serum HCY increases with age in Thoroughbred geldings, and that age should be considered when interpreting equine HCY.

title: Computed Tomographic Arthrography, Gross Anatomy, and Histology of the Tarsometatarsal Joint-Proximal Suspensory Ligament Relationship in Cadaveric Equine Hindlimbs: Absence of Synovial Communication.
journal: Veterinary and comparative orthopaedics and traumatology : V.C.O.T
abstract: The purpose of this study was to evaluate the presence of synovial invaginations from the tarsometatarsal joint (TMT) into the proximal suspensory ligament (PSL) in cadaveric equine hindlimbs using CT arthrography, macroscopic examination, and histological analysis. The hypothesis was that synovial invaginations, as reported in forelimbs, would be present in hindlimbs. A secondary objective was to describe the plantar recesses of the TMT joint. Eight frozen-thawed cadaveric equine hindlimbs underwent TMT joint injection with 3 mL of contrast medium and methylene blue (1:1). CT images were evaluated for contrast enhancement within the PSL. Gross dissection focused on detecting methylene blue. The proximal 3 cm of the PSL from five fresh hindlimbs was histologically examined for synovial membrane tissue. Plantar recess CT visualization frequency was recorded. One limb (1/8) was excluded due to inadvertent injection of the perforating tarsal vein. Contrast medium and methylene blue were absent within the PSL in all included limbs (0/7). Four plantar recesses were identified with variable frequency: A (5/7), B (5/7), C (3/7), and D (7/7). Histological examination confirmed the absence of synovial membrane tissue in all examined limbs (0/5). In contrast to forelimbs, where synovial invaginations are consistently present, this study demonstrates the absence of synovial communication between the TMT joint and PSL in hindlimbs, requiring region-specific clinical approaches.

title: Insights into mare lactation and foal nutrition in horses: physiological, nutritional, and genetic regulation of milk composition for foal-rearing management.
abstract: Mare lactation contributes to foal nutrition, passive immune transfer, growth, hydration, and gastrointestinal development. However, lactation adequacy cannot be evaluated from milk composition alone because foal outcomes also depend on colostrum intake, suckling ability, intestinal absorption, maternal condition, and postnatal management. This review critically analyzes equine colostrum, mare milk composition, maternal nutrition, genetic and molecular regulation, microbiome interactions, and foal-rearing practices. Milk yield and composition vary with lactation stage, breed, parity, age, body condition, diet, and management, limiting the usefulness of fixed reference values. Molecular and multi-omics studies have broadened our understanding of mare milk, but much of the evidence remains descriptive, with limited links to measured foal outcomes. Future studies should integrate standardized mare-milk-foal phenotyping and longitudinal monitoring, while validating digital measures of nursing behavior against established assessments of passive transfer and defined growth, gastrointestinal, and weaning outcomes.

title: A rare case of equine pulmonary and encephalic cryptococcosis with progressive neurologic disease.
abstract: A 6-year-old neutered male Quarter Horse was presented with a 15-day history of progressive neurological dysfunction characterized by gait incoordination, visual impairment, ptosis, head tilt, tetraparesis, and eventual recumbency. Transient improvement followed corticosteroid therapy; however, neurological deterioration occurred, and euthanasia was elected. At necropsy, a focal, well-demarcated, yellow gelatinous lesion was identified in the ventral mesencephalon. A firm pulmonary nodule was also observed in the right caudal lung lobe, containing a central cavity filled with yellow gelatinous material. Histologically, the brainstem lesion consisted of severe, focally extensive pyogranulomatous encephalitis associated with numerous encapsulated yeasts measuring 6-25 μm in diameter. The pulmonary nodule consisted of a fibrotic lesion containing similar fungal structures and necrotic debris. Organisms stained positively with periodic acid-Schiff, Grocott's methenamine silver, Fontana-Masson, and Alcian blue. Nested polymerase chain reaction targeting the conserved internal transcribed spacer region confirmed Cryptococcus spp. A diagnosis of pulmonary and encephalic cryptococcosis was established, highlighting the diagnostic value of necropsy and histopathology in a rare equine presentation of the disease.

title: Wearable automated cough detection in horses with chronic cough: model development, validation, and exploratory associations in asthma.
abstract: Coughing is a nonspecific respiratory sign that is common in horses with asthma. Cough quantification is currently subjective and labor-intensive, leaving its diagnostic and monitoring potential underexplored. (1) Develop a wearable audio recorder for horses; (2) collect recordings of coughing horses and annotate coughs; (3) train a machine learning model to automate cough detection; and (4) describe temporal patterns of coughing and determine pathophysiologic correlations in horses with asthma. Seventy horses were recruited from a teaching herd, clinical cases, and via social media. Sixty had coughing for ≥3 weeks and valid recordings. In our prospective observational and analytical study, coughs were recorded using a digital device, annotated by a single observer, and used to develop a machine-learning-based cough-detection pipeline. Machine learning output was analyzed using generalized linear mixed models to determine circadian patterns and pathophysiologic associations of coughing. We annotated 252 of 1260 recorded hours. We labeled 8555 sound events, 2780 of which were coughs of the instrumented horse. Our machine learning model detected coughs with a sensitivity of 0.95 and a specificity of 0.9993. In horses with asthma, coughing frequency was associated with neutrophilic lung inflammation and showed a diurnal pattern with peak rates around 3 am. The combination of robust hardware for long-term recordings and high-performance machine learning algorithms has the potential to transform coughing from a relatively crude clinical sign to a quantifiable endpoint in research and clinical practice.

title: Present-day spatial differentiation and associated factors of Meishan traditional villages in Central Hunan.
abstract: Central Hunan represents an important area of Meishan culture and a historical land-water transfer zone associated with the Ancient Tea Horse Road. Using 19 traditional villages in Anhua and Xinhua, this study examines spatial differentiation from the combined perspective of historical commercial corridors and local cultural institutions. Fourteen indicators were integrated with field observation and spatial analysis to characterize four exploratory village types: Riverside Commercial, Mountain Settlement, Terraced Farming, and Cultural Node. One-way ANOVA showed significant between-type differences across seven core indicators. Geodetector analysis identified recorded distance to the historical tea-trade corridor (q = 0.814), route-remnant length (q = 0.805), and tourism development intensity (q = 0.713) as the strongest single-factor associations. Because of sparse cross-strata, only two pairwise interactions were reliably estimable. Threshold screening based on a predefined adjacent-grade Δq ≥ 0.15 rule was met by five of seven factors, whereas terrain slope and ritual-site density did not meet the criterion. These findings indicate that commercial-corridor accessibility, cultural carriers, environmental constraints, and contemporary socio-economic conditions are associated with present-day spatial differentiation among the villages. The study provides an evidence-based basis for differentiated conservation of traditional villages in the Meishan cultural region while explicitly recognizing the limitations of the small sample and exploratory threshold analysis.

title: Postoperative intravenous lidocaine after small intestinal surgery in horses: The CHARIOT randomised clinical trial.
abstract: Postoperative reflux (POR) is common following surgical treatment of colic and is associated with increased mortality, prolonged hospitalisation and higher treatment costs. To evaluate the clinical efficacy of intravenous lidocaine administered for 48-72 h postoperatively in horses following surgical treatment of small intestinal obstruction. Randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind multicentre superiority clinical trial. Eligible horses undergoing emergency laparotomy to treat acute colic caused by small intestinal obstruction at participating hospitals (UK n = 7, Belgium n = 1) were randomised 1:1 to receive a continuous intravenous infusion of lidocaine or saline placebo for 48 (minimum) to 72 (maximum) h following surgery and anaesthetic recovery. The primary outcome was the proportion of horses that developed POR during the infusion (≥2 L net reflux on ≥2 occasions). Secondary outcomes included other measures of gastrointestinal function and systemic patient status, surgical morbidities, short- and long-term postoperative mortality, and occurrence of adverse events. A significantly greater proportion of horses developed POR in the lidocaine (55/137, 40.1%) compared to the placebo group (41/140, 29.3%) (adjusted relative risk 1.51, 95% confidence interval 1.10-2.08; p = 0.011). Total reflux volume was greater in the lidocaine group (median 2 L vs. 0 L; p = 0.047). No statistically significant between-group differences were observed for all other secondary outcomes. Infusion-related serious adverse events occurred in 4 (1.4%) horses, all in the lidocaine group; non-serious adverse events occurred in 23 (8.3%) horses. Serum lidocaine concentrations and hepatic function were not measured. Intraoperative lidocaine administration was not randomised. In horses undergoing emergency laparotomy for small intestinal obstruction, the proportion that developed POR was higher in horses receiving postoperative lidocaine infusion for 48-72 h compared with placebo. These findings do not support routine postoperative lidocaine use to improve return of gastrointestinal function or other clinical outcomes in this surgical population.

title: Effect of discontinuing a constant rate intravenous infusion of lidocaine on recovery from general anesthesia with isoflurane in horses: A randomized clinical trial.
abstract: To evaluate the effect of discontinuing intravenous (IV) lidocaine infusions 30 minutes before the end of inhalational anesthesia on recovery from general anesthesia in horses. Randomized controlled clinical study. A group of 40 healthy adult horses undergoing general anesthesia for magnetic resonance imaging. All horses underwent a standard anesthetic protocol. Lidocaine was injected IV as a loading dose (2 mg kg-1), followed by a continuous rate IV infusion of 3 mg kg-1 hour-1. Horses were randomly allocated to one of two groups: discontinuation of the infusion 30 minutes before the end of anesthesia (group DC, n = 20), or continuation until the end of anesthesia (group C, n = 20). A three-axis accelerometer was secured around the withers to obtain accelerometry-based recovery scores (RS). Lower scores correlate with higher-quality recovery and higher scores correlate with lower-quality recovery. Recorded variables included time to first movement, time to sternal recumbency, time to standing and number of standing attempts. RS (mean ± standard deviation) was analyzed using a Student's t-test. Significance was set at p < 0.05. Mean RS were 22 ± 7 and 25 ± 8 for groups C and DC, respectively (p = 0.175). Median times to first movement, sternal recumbency and standing were 43 (21-69), 56 (29-90) and 61 (29-111) minutes for group C, and 33 (21-69), 45 (26-97) and 50 (36-97) minutes for group DC, respectively. The median number of stand attempts was 1 (1-5) for both groups. Discontinuing lidocaine infusions 30 minutes before the end of inhalational anesthesia did not improve recovery quality compared with infusions continued until the end. These findings do not support a benefit of early lidocaine discontinuation in this context.

title: Seasonal Dermoscopic Findings in Aged Equines With Haircoat Shedding Dysfunction Versus Aged Equines With Normal Annual Shedding Patterns.
abstract: Dermoscopy can be used to assess hair density (trichoscopy). The effects of seasonal variations and abnormalities in shedding on hair density are unknown. To compare prospectively the variations in jugular hair shaft density (JHD) in aged equines over the four seasons, and in groups with normal haircoat and moulting (NORM) versus abnormal haircoat and shedding patterns (ABN). Client-owned equines, ≥ 15 years old. A standardised clinical examination and a questionnaire for shedding history were carried out. A dermoscopy was performed once at the midpoint of the jugular groove using a handheld device connected to a smartphone. Hair shafts per cm2 were counted using ImageJ software. Statistical analyses were conducted using the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney U and Kruskal-Wallis tests. Of the 138 enrolled cases, aged between 15 and 44 years, 90 (65.2%) were NORM and 48 (34.8%) ABN. JHD was highest in winter (median 701 hairs/cm2, interquartile range (IQR) 637-845) and lowest in summer (median 637 hairs/cm2, IQR 548-715), with a significant difference between seasons (p = 0.05). JHD did not differ between ponies and horses. JHD was significantly higher in ABN (median 760 hairs/cm2, IQR 683-913) than in NORM (median 639 hairs/cm2, IQR 547-711). Scales and skin debris were frequently observed in the ABN group. Dermoscopy is useful for assessing hair density in the field. JHD varies with the seasons, enabling the haircoat to adapt appropriately. Observable abnormalities in the moulting process, particularly delayed shedding and persistent hair, which may accompany certain systemic diseases, including pituitary pars intermedia dysfunction, are accompanied by an increase in hair density in the jugular region.

title: Consistent Across Studies, Divergent Across Outcomes: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis of Animal-Assisted Interventions for Autism Spectrum Disorder.
journal: Autism : the international journal of research and practice
abstract: Animal-assisted interventions (AAI) have gained attention as complementary approaches for autistic individuals, yet overall efficacy and moderator influences remain unclear. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched through March 2026 for controlled trials reporting behavioral outcomes in autism spectrum disorder. A three-level model accounted for dependent effect sizes nested within studies. Subgroup analyses, meta-regression, publication bias, and Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) certainty assessments were conducted. Seventeen studies (159 effect sizes; 677 unique participants) entered the meta-analysis. The overall effect was small but significant (g = 0.275, 95% confidence interval [CI] [0.153, 0.397], p < .001), with heterogeneity entirely within studies (I2_Level 2 = 32.2%, I2_Level 3 = 0%). Social functioning (g = 0.337) was most consistently supported; communication (g = 0.597) and sensory outcomes (g = 0.590) showed the largest effects. No moderator predicted effect variation. Publication bias was not detected. Randomized controlled trial evidence was rated low certainty (GRADE). AAI-predominantly equestrian-based-produces a small, significant effect on behavioral outcomes in primarily autistic children and adolescents, consistent across studies but varying by outcome domain. Low certainty of evidence warrants cautious interpretation and underscores the need for rigorous, adequately powered trials.Lay AbstractAAI, such as therapeutic horseback riding and dog-assisted therapy, are increasingly used to support autistic children and adolescents. We combined findings from 17 studies involving 677 participants to examine whether these interventions improve behavioral outcomes. Overall, we found a small but meaningful positive effect, particularly for social skills. Communication and sensory outcomes showed promising but less certain improvements. Most studies focused on horse-based programs, so more research is needed on other animal types. The quality of evidence was rated as low, meaning we cannot be fully confident in these findings. Larger, more rigorous studies are needed, and future research should include the perspectives of autistic individuals in designing and evaluating these programs.

title: Transverse intervertebral ratios of computed tomographic myelography of the caudal cervical spine (C5-C7) are a reliable diagnostic parameter in horses with ataxia caused by enlarged caudal intervertebral articular process joints.
abstract: Computed tomographic myelography (CTM) is increasingly used in horses with spinal ataxia. However, objective parameters for determining clinically significant spinal cord compression are lacking. To evaluate ratios on cross-sectional CTM images as a diagnostic parameter for cervical spinal cord compression at the level of the caudal articular process joints. Retrospective, comparative cross-sectional study. Horses with spinal ataxia (Group A; n = 33) and control horses with no clinical evidence of neurologic disease (Group N; n = 19) were examined clinically and underwent CTM. On transverse images at the caudal articular process joints (APJs) of C5 to C7, the cord canal area ratio (CCAR), the contrast-enhanced cord canal area ratio (CE-CCAR), and the contrast-enhanced cord area ratio (CE-CAR) were calculated and compared between groups. Histopathological findings from post-mortem (p.m.) examinations were included if the results were available. Significant differences were identified for CCAR (mean ratio A2: 0.21-0.22 vs. mean ratio N: 0.18-0.19; p = 0.01-0.04) and CE-CAR (mean ratio A2: 0.36-0.4 vs. mean ratio N: 0.32-0.34; p = 0.005-0.01) at the caudal cervical spine between affected and control horses. Optimal cut-off values to detect clinically significant cervical cord compression using CE-CAR were between 0.33 and 0.44, with a sensitivity of 50% to 100% (95% confidence intervals [CIs] between 15% and 100%); and specificity of 42%-100% (95% CIs between 17% and 100%) when compared with p.m. examination results. Limited number of control horses and incomplete p.m. data to confirm spinal cord pathology for all cases. The CE-CAR supports the identification of cervical spinal cord compression and enhances consistency in objective image interpretation. It is a valuable ratio for determining the clinical significance of spinal cord compression in the caudal cervical spine using CTM.

title: Associations between adiponectin, leptin/adiponectin ratio, insulin dysregulation and pre-existing laminitis in light breed horses.
abstract: Hypoadiponectinaemia is associated with insulin dysregulation (ID) and pre-existing laminitis (PEL) in ponies, but this relationship has not been thoroughly investigated in horses. To characterise the relationship between serum adiponectin, leptin, the leptin/adiponectin (L/A) ratio, ID and PEL in a cohort of light breed horses. Cross-sectional study. Horses (n = 720) with and without ID and PEL were investigated. Logistic and linear regressions were performed to assess the relationship between adiponectin, leptin, the L/A ratio, ID and PEL. Median [IQR] adiponectin (μg/mL) was higher (p < 0.001) for horses without ID (8.4 [6.7-10.8]) compared to those with ID (6.1 [4.5-8.9]) and for horses without PEL (8.3 [6.8-10.6] compared to those with PEL (6.3 [4.7-8.7]). Median L/A ratio was lower (p < 0.001) in horses without ID (0.8 [0.4-1.3]) compared to those with ID (1.9 [1.2-2.9]) and for horses without PEL (0.8 [0.5-1.7]) compared to those with PEL (1.7 [0.9-2.6]. Adiponectin was negatively associated with ID (OR [95% CI] = 0.8 [0.8-0.9], p < 0.001) and PEL (0.8 [0.7-0.9], p < 0.001). Leptin was positively associated with ID (1.1 [1.1-1.2], p < 0.001), but not PEL (p = 0.5). The L/A ratio was positively associated (p < 0.001) with both ID (3.0 [2.2-4.3]) and PEL (1.7 [1.3-2.3). Using 1.2 as a cut-off, L/A ratio was 76% (68-82) sensitive and 74% (66-81) specific for diagnosis of ID. Cross-sectional design limits interpretation of associations. Hypoadiponectinaemia and increased L/A ratio are associated with ID and PEL in light breed horses and warrant further clinical evaluation as biomarkers of laminitis risk.

title: Economic impact of epizootic lymphangitis in cart pulling horses in a low-income setting.
abstract: Epizootic lymphangitis (EL) is a contagious fungal disease threatening the health and welfare of working equids and the economic stability of dependent communities in resource-constrained settings. To assess owner clinical awareness regarding EL and to quantify the direct and indirect household-level financial losses attributable to the disease in an urban working carthorse population. Observational cross-sectional survey. Structured questionnaire interviews were conducted with 285 carthorse owners in Gondar town, Ethiopia. Descriptive statistics, financial loss modelling (converted to USD at 1 USD ≈ 133.33 ETB), and multivariable logistic regression were applied to evaluate disease awareness, economic impact drivers, and socio-demographic predictors. Near-universal clinical symptom recognition was observed among respondents (94.04%), yet a profound educational gap existed, with 65.85% unaware of the underlying microbial aetiology. The mean overall financial loss was $508.05 (67,739.41 ETB) per household per year. Primary financial loss drivers were equine mortality ($306.78 [40,903.85 ETB]) and forced premature culling ($175.63 [23,416.67 ETB]). Reduced draught power capacity, opportunity cost of family labour, carcass disposal, and isolation facility costs contributed $14.69 (1959.35 ETB), $4.35 (579.74 ETB), $2.61 (347.58 ETB), and $2.61 (347.58 ETB), respectively. Out-of-pocket veterinary treatment ($0.51 [68.53 ETB]) and supplementary feeding ($0.66 [87.90 ETB]) represented negligible fractions of total losses. Owners with secondary education exhibited significantly higher odds of epidemiological awareness (OR = 4.46, 95% CI: 2.27-9.45, p < 0.001). Nonrandomised convenience sampling across urban cart stations may introduce selection bias, while reliance on 12-month owner recall introduces potential reporting inaccuracies for minor operational expenses. While clinical recognition of EL cutaneous lesions is exceptionally high, a critical knowledge deficit persists regarding its aetiology and transmission dynamics. Veterinary outreach programmes must pair clinical disease management with targeted biosecurity education to address epidemiological misconceptions and mitigate these substantial economic shocks.

title: Dynamic gestational changes in quantitative and qualitative platelet indices in Spanish Purebred mares.
abstract: Platelet (PLT) indices during pregnancy are well described in women and partially characterized in cattle and sheep but remain poorly investigated in mares. This study evaluated quantitative and qualitative platelet indices in healthy pregnant and non-pregnant Spanish Purebred mares. Blood samples from 30 mares (20 pregnant and 10 non-pregnant), aged 4-17 years, were analyzed using an ADVIA 2120i hematology analyzer. Quantitative platelet indices [PLT, PCT, MPV, LARGEPLT, and AGREG] and qualitative indices related to platelet heterogeneity, composition, and mass [PDW, MPC, MPM, PCDW, and PMDW] were evaluated using Mann-Whitney U tests and mixed-effects models. Non-pregnant mares exhibited higher PLT counts than pregnant mares (p < 0.05), whereas no significant differences were detected for the remaining indices. Longitudinal analysis revealed significant gestational variation in PLT, MPV, LARGEPLT, PDW, PCDW, and PMDW. PLT counts were higher during months 8-10 than during months 2-6. MPV was higher at month 8 than at month 7, whereas LARGEPLT was higher at month 9 than during months 4-6 and 8 and peaked at month 11. PDW, PCDW, and PMDW showed highest values during mid- to late gestation (p < 0.05). In contrast, PCT, MPC, MPM, and AGREG showed no significant gestational effects. Correlation analysis revealed strong associations among platelet size-, mass-, and heterogeneity-related indices. These findings indicate that equine pregnancy is associated with dynamic changes in platelet indices, particularly those related to platelet size and heterogeneity. These patterns provide baseline information on platelet adaptations during equine gestation and improve understanding of pregnancy-related hematological changes in mares.

title: Perioperative serum zinc dynamics in Thoroughbred racehorses undergoing orthopedic surgery.
abstract: This study evaluated perioperative serum zinc dynamics in Thoroughbred racehorses undergoing orthopedic surgery. Based on the procedure type, 17 horses were classified as having undergone arthroscopic surgery (n = 11) or internal fixation (n = 6). Serum samples were collected during preoperative preparation, at wound suturing, and on postoperative days 1 and 3. In the arthroscopic surgery group, serum zinc concentrations significantly decreased during surgery and on postoperative day 1, with recovery by postoperative day 3. The internal fixation group had lower zinc levels at baseline, and no significant changes were observed. Taken together, these findings suggest that perioperative zinc dynamics are influenced by surgical factors as well as differences in the underlying injury and associated inflammatory status.

title: Stereotypic behavior in horses: An integrative model linking management, welfare, performance, and suitability for companion and equine-assisted roles.
abstract: The growth of intensive management systems in the horse industry has raised concern about equine welfare. Confinement simplifies feeding, health control, and athletic preparation, but can also restrict natural behavior and favor stereotypic behaviors such as crib-biting, weaving, and stall-walking, behaviors widely regarded as indicators associated with current or previous management-related welfare compromise, although established stereotypies can persist after the initial adverse conditions have changed. This review proposes an integrative pathway model linking management deficits, stereotypic behavior, and three downstream domains: physical health, athletic performance, and suitability for companion and equine-assisted intervention roles. Unlike prior narrative summaries that treat these domains separately, the model incorporates individual moderators, such as temperament and coping style, that help explain why reported associations vary across studies, and pairs this with a structured narrative appraisal of evidence quality and consistency in each domain, based on expert judgment of study design, directness, replication, and consistency rather than a formal systematic quality-assessment tool (see Section 2). The evidence linking stereotypic behavior to health and welfare outcomes is comparatively strong and consistent across populations. The evidence linking it to athletic performance is more limited, largely observational, and influenced by individual temperament. The evidence on suitability for companion and assisted work is the sparsest of the three and, in at least one study, contradicts the assumption that horses with a stereotypy history are systematically less suited for such roles. These findings support management strategies that prioritize natural behavior while identifying where current causal claims outpace the evidence.

title: Therapeutic approaches in two cases of leukoencephalomalacia in creole horses.
abstract: Equine leukoencephalomalacia (ELEM) is a highly lethal encephalopathy associated with the ingestion of corn contaminated with Fusarium spp., causing liquefactive necrosis of cerebral white matter. This study reports the intensive therapeutic management and clinical recovery of two Criollo mares with suspected ELEM. Both animals originated from a farm experiencing an outbreak with 12 previous fatalities and postmortem confirmation of ELEM in affected horses. Diagnosis in the surviving mares was based on epidemiological history and neurological signs, including blindness, stupor, ataxia, dysphagia, and lower lip flaccidity. Intensive supportive treatment was administered for 10 days, including fluid therapy, anti-inflammatory drugs, antimicrobials, proton-pump inhibitors, vitamin supplementation, activated charcoal, and laminitis prophylaxis. Despite severe neurological impairment and a guarded prognosis, both mares achieved complete clinical recovery following intensive supportive care. These findings highlight the potential importance of early therapeutic intervention and continuous monitoring in managing suspected ELEM cases in horses.

title: Epilepsy and trigeminal neuralgia as regional hyperexcitability syndromes: converging mechanisms and translational insights from equine trigeminal-mediated headshaking.
abstract: Epilepsy and trigeminal neuralgia (TN) are treated traditionally as unrelated disorders, one defined by recurrent seizures, the other by paroxysmal facial pain. Yet both share a core pathophysiological feature: regional loss of neuronal excitability control, driven by gain-of-function in voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav1.3, Nav1.6, Nav1.7); failure of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)ergic inhibition, disruption of the blood-brain and blood-nerve barriers with transforming growth factor-β-mediated neuroinflammation; and emergent network hypersynchrony. Pharmacologically, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, gabapentin and baclofen act across both conditions; neuromodulation with repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation reduces excitability in epileptic foci and trigeminocervical circuits alike. Equine trigeminal-mediated headshaking (TMHS) presents as a spontaneous large-animal phenotype that matches this framework; affected horses show infraorbital trigeminal activation thresholds below 5 mA without structural lesion, seasonal and exercise-dependent fluctuation in clinical signs and partial response to percutaneous electrical nerve stimulation and magnesium supplementation. This narrative review synthesizes mechanistic evidence across epilepsy, TN and TMHS and maps their phenotypic overlap with related primary headache syndromes. It is proposed that all three conditions are best conceptualized as regional hyperexcitability syndromes differing primarily by network location and access to peripheral modulators such as posture, cervical biomechanics and autonomic tone. Recognizing this convergence supports cross-species therapeutic strategies targeting ion channels, inflammatory signalling, barrier stability and network-level neuromodulation, and identifies TMHS as a clinically tractable, welfare-relevant translational model.

title: Hippotherapy for the social communication of children with ASD: An exploratory randomized clinical trial.
authors: de Melo Bezerra Fontoura Larissa Brenda
journal: Folia phoniatrica et logopaedica : official organ of the International Association of Logopedics and Phoniatrics (IALP)
abstract: Hippotherapy has emerged as a promising complementary approach, offering rich sensorimotor and social experiences that may enhance communication outcomes in children with ASD. However, despite growing interest in equine-assisted interventions, there is a scarcity of robust randomized clinical trials examining structured speech-language programs focused on social communication within hippotherapy settings. This study aimed to investigate the effectiveness of the Step-by-Step in Communication program (a standardized speech-language intervention used in hippotherapy) in improving communicative and linguistic skills in children with ASD. Randomized clinical trial with 49 children aged 2 to 6 years diagnosed with ASD. Participants were randomly assigned to two groups: G1 (one session per week for 24 weeks) and G2 (two sessions per week for 12 weeks), both totaling 24 sessions. The intervention followed the Step-by-Step in Communication program. Outcomes were assessed using the Behavioral Observation Protocol (PROC) and the Autism Treatment Evaluation Checklist (ATEC). Both groups' language skills improved significantly intragroup, as measured by PROC, and reduced significantly three ATEC domains, whereas no significant changes were observed in the Health/Physical/Behavior domain. Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), controlling for baseline scores, revealed no significant differences between groups and their intervention conditions. These findings suggest that hippotherapy may be an effective complementary intervention for improving language and autism-related outcomes in children with ASD. Different weekly intervention frequencies with the same total number of sessions did not appear to influence final outcomes; hence, the program may be implemented with different weekly schedules without compromising its effectiveness.

title: Alterations in dopaminergic activity in the large intestine of horses with pituitary pars intermedia dysfunction.
abstract: Pituitary pars intermedia dysfunction (PPID) is a neurogenerative disorder in horses characterised by dopaminergic neuronal loss, resembling Parkinson's disease. While Parkinson's disease involves dopaminergic degeneration in both the brain and the gut, intestinal involvement in PPID has not been investigated. This study aims to investigate dopaminergic activity in the enteric nervous system (ENS) of the large intestine in horses with PPID. Archived intestinal samples from horses with PPID (pituitary grade 4/5 or 5/5 with clinical signs consistent with PPID) and aged controls (pituitary grade 1/5 or 2/5) were used. Expression of tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) and dopamine receptor-2 (D2R) were measured in the ENS of the caecum, large colon, and small colon by immunohistochemistry. Quantification of positive staining was performed on 8 ganglia per sample and averaged. Statistical comparisons were made using unpaired t-test or Mann-Whitney test for group difference, and one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) or Kruskal-Wallis test across intestinal segments. Horses with PPID showed significantly lower TH expressions in the submucosal plexus of the caecum (control vs. PPID: 1.97% [0-16.52] vs. 0.03% [0-0.46], P = 0.042), and significantly higher D2R expression in both the submucosal plexus (0.66% [0.04-1.23] vs. 3.86% [0.06-8.93], P = 0.011) and myenteric plexus (0.28% [0.03-2.34] vs. 1.50% [0.77-5.76], P = 0.045) of the caecum. These findings provide novel evidence of altered dopaminergic signalling in the equine gut in PPID, suggesting enteric involvement in disease pathophysiology. Further research into enteric glial function and D2R targeted therapies are warranted.

title: ASSOCIATION BETWEEN AIRBORNE PATHOGENS AND PERFORMANCE IN STANDARDBRED RACEHORSES.
abstract: The association between airway pathogens and mild-moderate equine asthma has been described, unlike their potential influence on exercise. The objective was to investigate association between detection of airway pathogens and racing performance. The retrospective cohort study involved 122 racing Trotters, excluding horses with signs of systemic illness. Tracheal wash (TW) and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) were performed for cytology and fungal culture; bacterial culture and qPCR (Mycoplasma, viruses) were also performed on TW. Clinical status was defined based on clinical signs and BAL fluid cytology and included as a covariate for statistical analysis. Performance was assessed (univariable/multivariable logistic regressions) on mean earnings per race, ratio of wins and podiums for the race immediately preceding/following sampling, and during 3-month periods before/after sampling. Equine Rhinitis B virus (ERBV), equine herpesvirus-2 (EHV-2) and EHV-5 were detected in TW of 50/122 (40.9%), 36/122 (29.5%) and 46/122 horses (37.7%), respectively. Mycoplasma spp. was detected in 54/122 (44.3%), and bacterial culture was positive for 9/122 (7.4%) horses. ERBV detection was significantly negatively associated with performance on the next race (OR_podium: 0.18 [0.05-0.61]; p = 0.006), while no association was found for other time periods. No association with performance was found for other viruses, Mycoplasma spp. and fungal culture. Positive bacterial culture was positively associated with performance during the preceding 3-month period (OR_top25%_victories: 32.8 [3.94-273.6]; p = 0.001), while no association was found for other periods. ERBV was the only virus with significant influence on short-term performance. None of the respiratory pathogens exhibited longer (3-month scale) consequences.

title: SNP Profiling of TBX3 and GHR Genes: Association with Conformation Traits Variation in the Turkmen-Thoroughbred Crossbred Horses.
abstract: Unlocking the genetic architecture of equine biometric traits is pivotal for optimizing breeding strategies and athletic performance. This study investigated the association of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the T-box transcription factor 3 (TBX3) and growth hormone receptor (GHR) genes-two key regulators of skeletal development and metabolism-with different traits within a population of 103 Turkmen × Thoroughbred crossbred horses. Utilizing PCR-SSCP and targeted sequencing, we identified two SNPs in the TBX3 flanking region: PV184589T>C and PV184589G>A (correspond to rs1151596815). Notably, the PV184589T>C variant altered the frequency of ZESTE_CS regulatory motifs, suggesting a functional role in modulating TBX3 expression and downstream osteogenic pathways. While the GHR locus remained monomorphic in this population, association analysis revealed that TBX3 genotypes significantly influence critical morphometric parameters, including neck circumference at throat latch (NCTL), fore pastern length (FPL), forearm circumference (FAMC), croup to dock length (CD) and hind coronet circumference (HCC) (p<0.05). These results underscore TBX3 as a potent molecular marker for structural conformation and body size in horses, although validation in independent and larger populations is required before it can be considered for marker-assisted selection. By bridging the gap between regulatory genomics and phenotypic variation, the findings provide a precise genetic tool for marker-assisted selection, particularly in crossbred populations where athletic versatility and structural integrity are paramount.

title: Myoglobin-dependent regulation of mitochondrial bioenergetics and glucose metabolism in murine C2C12 skeletal muscle myotubes.
abstract: Lactate (LAC) accumulates in skeletal muscle when production surpasses utilization and tissue export during exercise. Recent biochemical studies have revealed that increasing LAC concentrations reduce oxygen (O2) binding to equine skeletal muscle myoglobin (Mb). To determine whether LAC-Mb associations affect cellular metabolism, we treated three variants of the C2C12 mouse skeletal muscle myotubes - Mb wild-type (MbWT), Mb knockout (MbKO) and Mb empty vector (MbEV) - with varying concentrations of sodium l-lactate (1.8-8.0 mM) for 3-24 h to assess net LAC uptake, net glucose (GLU) uptake and mitochondrial bioenergetics. Intracellular LAC levels increased in all LAC-treated Mb genotype variants but not in control cells. After 24 h, net GLU uptake was significantly higher in MbKO cells than in MbWT or MbEV cells. At 6 h, mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation contributed ∼70% of total ATP production in LAC-treated MbWT and MbEV cells. However, at 24 h, a higher (∼57%-67%) contribution of glycolysis-derived ATP was recorded. Total ATP production was significantly lower (∼35%) in MbKO cells at both 6 and 24 h, largely due to lower glycolysis-derived ATP production (∼26%-31%). Our findings support the concept that Mb plays a role in modulating skeletal muscle GLU uptake, glycolytic versus oxidative metabolism and total ATP production. Notably, Mb-associated effects appear to be LAC-independent, at least in the C2C12 cell model. Overall, these results are consistent with a growing body of evidence pointing to multiple physiological and regulatory functions for Mb, including cellular fuel trafficking and regulation of mitochondrial function.

title: Hyperimmune immunoglobulin for people with COVID-19.
journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
abstract: Hyperimmune intravenous immunoglobulin (hIVIG) is a preparation of polyclonal antibodies obtained from pooled convalescent plasma or immunised animals. It is a potential therapy for coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). This review update focusses on hIVIG. It emanates from a 2021 parent review investigating convalescent plasma and hIVIG for people with COVID-19. To assess the benefits and harms of hIVIG therapy for people with COVID-19, and to maintain evidence currency using a living systematic review approach. We searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, the Epistemonikos COVID-19 L*OVE Platform, and clinical trial registries from 1 January 2019 onwards. We conducted searches on 15 December 2024. We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated hIVIG for COVID-19, irrespective of participants' disease severity, age, gender, or ethnicity. We excluded other coronavirus disease studies, and those evaluating standard immunoglobulin. We used the GRADE approach to rate the certainty of evidence for all-cause mortality, clinical status or symptom resolution, quality of life, adverse events, grade 3-4 adverse events, and serious adverse events. We used the RoB 2 tool to assess bias in the RCTs. We followed standard Cochrane methodology. We included eight new RCTs in this update, for a total of 13 included studies with 3374 participants. Of these, 1511 participants received hIVIG from humans, 547 received swine glyco-humanised polyclonal antibody, 1075 received a bovine-derived polyclonal preparation, and 241 received equine-derived polyclonal antibody (EpAb). Three RCTs included participants with asymptomatic or mild disease, one included participants with mild to moderate disease, and nine included participants with moderate to severe disease. We identified eight ongoing studies and nine studies awaiting assessment. We summarise key results for three prioritised comparisons below. The main review presents five comparisons (including these three) in summary of findings tables, and all analysed comparisons (including additional dose ranges of hIVIG and animal-derived polyclonal antibodies), with some results presented in supplementary tables. Participants with moderate to severe disease Benefits of human-derived hIVIG hIVIG may have little to no impact on all-cause mortality at 28 days (risk ratio (RR) 0.75, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.45 to 1.24; low-certainty evidence). The evidence is very uncertain about the effect on worsening of clinical status by day 7 (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.23; very low-certainty evidence). It may have little to no impact on improvement of clinical status by day 28 (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.08; low-certainty evidence). No studies reported on quality of life. Harms of human-derived hIVIG hIVIG may have little to no impact on adverse events (any grade) by day 28 (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.19; 449 per 1000; 2 studies, 599 participants; low-certainty evidence). Participants receiving hIVIG probably experience more grade 3-4 adverse events than those given placebo (RR 4.09, 95% CI 1.39 to 12.01; moderate-certainty evidence). hIVIG therapy may have little to no effect on serious adverse events or death by day 28 (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.14; 96 per 1000; 1 study, 572 participants; low-certainty evidence). Benefits of equine-derived polyclonal antibody (EpAb) EpAb may reduce all-cause mortality at 28 days (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.26 to 1.37; low-certainty evidence). EpAb may reduce worsening of clinical status by day 28 (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.38 to 1.18; low-certainty evidence). It may improve clinical status by day 28 (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.17; low-certainty evidence). No studies reported on quality of life. Harms of EpAb EpAb may have little to no impact on the number of adverse events (any grade) by day 28 (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.31; low-certainty evidence). Grade 3-4 adverse events were not reported. EpAb may reduce serious adverse events (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.38 to 1.19; low-certainty evidence). Participants with asymptomatic or mild disease Benefits of human-derived hIVIG We do not know whether hIVIG has any impact on all-cause mortality at 28 days (RR not estimable as no events; very low-certainty evidence). hIVIG may have little to no effect on admission to hospital or death by day 28 (RR 2.38, 95% CI 0.63 to 9.03; low-certainty evidence). It may have little to no impact on symptom resolution by day 14 (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.21; low-certainty evidence). Quality of life was not reported. Harms of human-derived hIVIG hIVIG may have little to no impact on adverse events (any grade) by day 28 (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.18; low-certainty evidence). Grade 3-4 adverse events were not reported. hIVIG may have little to no effect on serious adverse events by day 28 (RR 2.38, 95% CI 0.63 to 9.03; low-certainty evidence). We included data from 13 RCTs that compared hIVIG to standard therapy or placebo. Clinical heterogeneity (e.g. human- and animal-derived preparations, varying doses and comparators) precluded pooling most of the studies. In moderate to severe disease, human-derived hIVIG may have little to no impact on mortality or clinical improvement. hIVIG may have little to no effect on adverse events of any grade and serious adverse events, and probably increases grade 3-4 adverse events. In moderate to severe disease, equine-derived polyclonal antibody may reduce mortality and clinical worsening, and may increase the number of people discharged at 28 days. EpAb may have little to no impact on adverse events at 28 days and may reduce serious adverse events. In asymptomatic to mild disease, the effect of human-derived hIVIG on mortality is very uncertain. It may have little to no impact on symptom resolution, adverse events (any grade), and serious adverse events. This is the second and final update of this living systematic review. We regularly searched for new evidence and updated the review as relevant studies became available. With funding expired and the need for a living approach no longer urgent, the review will be retired after this update. European Union Horizon 2020 research and innovation programme (grant agreement No. 101015756) REGISTRATION: The protocol was registered with the Center for Open Science on 17 April 2020.

title: Macrotyloma uniflorum: a comprehensive review on its nutritional profile and emerging therapeutic potential driven by bioactive peptides-generation methods and pharmacological significance.
abstract: Macrotyloma uniflorum (horse gram) is a drought tolerant legume of considerable nutritional and pharmacological value that remains underexploited relative to major pulses such as chickpea, lentil, and soybean. The seeds provide 15-22% protein along with substantial carbohydrate, dietary fibre, and micronutrient content, together with phenolics, flavonoids, tannins, and saponins that contribute to its broad pharmacological profile, including antidiabetic, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antiobesity, antimicrobial, antihypertensive, hepatoprotective, and antiurolithiatic activities. However, its dietary utilization is constrained by antinutritional factors such as phytic acid, tannins, trypsin inhibitors, and oligosaccharides that limit digestibility and mineral bioavailability, though processing methods such as soaking, germination, roasting, and fermentation can substantially reduce these compounds while enhancing phytochemical and antioxidant potential. Beyond its nutritional and phytochemical attributes, M. uniflorum proteins serve as precursors for bioactive peptides generated primarily through enzymatic hydrolysis, with additional contributions from chemical hydrolysis and microbial fermentation. Peptides such as TVGMTAKF and QLLLQQ, identified following Alcalase hydrolysis, retain antihypertensive activity after simulated gastrointestinal digestion. Fractionation via ultrafiltration, ion exchange chromatography, and gel filtration, combined with identification through MALDI-TOF and LC-MS/MS, has enabled characterization of peptides with antioxidant and ACE inhibitory properties, while in silico platforms such as BIOPEP-UWM and PeptideRanker offer complementary prediction tools that remain largely unapplied to this species. This review synthesizes the nutritional composition, pharmacological activities, antinutritional constraints, and processing strategies of M. uniflorum, with particular focus on the generation, fractionation, identification, and bioactivity of its protein derived peptides. Persistent gaps limited in vivo and clinical validation, scarce bioavailability and pharmacokinetic data, methodological inconsistency across studies, and minimal application of proteomic and computational prediction tools constrain translation of these findings into functional foods and nutraceuticals. Addressing these gaps through standardized processing, advanced peptidomic characterization, and clinical evaluation is essential to establishing M. uniflorum as a viable source of multifunctional bioactive peptides.

title: Biosecurity discourse among horse owners and veterinarians in the United Kingdom.
abstract: Despite its importance for disease prevention, biosecurity implementation across the equine industry remains inconsistent. Horse owners and veterinarians may describe biosecurity differently, which may shape how biosecurity advice is communicated and interpreted. Examining how biosecurity is talked about can provide insight into how it is described and understood within each group. To identify and compare patterns in how horse owners and veterinarians talk about biosecurity. Qualitative study situated within a post-structuralist framework. Individual semi-structured interviews were conducted with 23 horse owners and 14 veterinarians across the United Kingdom between December 2018 and November 2019. Transcripts were analysed using Foucauldian discourse analysis. Three patterns were identified: contrasting ways of framing biosecurity, differing accounts of responsibility for biosecurity, and expressions of distrust between veterinarians and horse owners. Both participant groups described biosecurity as difficult to implement but did so in contrasting ways, with veterinarians emphasising procedural complexity and population-level responsibility, and horse owners emphasising practical challenges and individualised care. Responsibilities were described using metaphors, hedging, and blame-shifting, with differing accounts of who was responsible for which tasks. Distrust between groups was evident in how participants talked about the other group, with frustration, scepticism, and dismissiveness appearing in both sets of accounts. Findings are based on accounts from a self-selected sample, do not represent direct observations of behaviour, and may not capture the range of ways in which biosecurity is talked about across the wider equine industry. Horse owners and veterinarians described biosecurity and responsibility in different ways, and distrust was evident in how each group talked about the other. These differences may be relevant to understanding challenges in communication between groups. Reflecting on how clients, responsibility, and expertise are talked about in everyday interactions may support more constructive and collaborative veterinary communications.

title: Evaluation of the treatment of equine glandular gastric disease with long-acting injectable omeprazole versus long-acting injectable omeprazole and sucralfate.
abstract: Equine glandular gastric disease (EGGD) is a significant cause of morbidity in horses and remains challenging to treat. Oral omeprazole combined with sucralfate is currently widely used; however, treatment success rates are variable. To compare healing and improvement rates of EGGD between long-acting injectable omeprazole (LAIO) with and without adjunctive sucralfate therapy. Randomised blinded prospective clinical study. Gastroscopy was performed under standing sedation. Group 1 received 4 mg/kg omeprazole by intramuscular injection once weekly for 4 weeks and 20 mg/kg sucralfate orally twice daily for 4 weeks. Group 2 received 4 mg/kg omeprazole by intramuscular injection once weekly for 4 weeks. Follow-up gastroscopy was performed 7 days after the final injection. Gastroscopy images were scored blinded to the treatment groups. In Group 1, 7 of 11 horses (63.6%) had no change in lesion grade, 2 of 11 (18.2%) worsened by one grade, and 2 of 11 (18.2%) improved by one grade. In Group 2, 6 of 10 horses (60%) had no change, 2 of 10 (20%) worsened by one grade, and 2 of 10 (20%) improved by one grade. This study lacked the power for successful statistical analysis, but was abandoned because horses became intolerant to injection leading to safety concerns. Effect size was negligible (ESGD r = 0.22; EGGD r = 0.00). Ten localised and self-limiting injection site reactions were observed in 6 horses treated with LAIO (12% of all injections). The study was discontinued before the planned sample size was reached because repeated injections posed an unacceptable safety risk to personnel. Small sample size, unequal baseline lesion severity, and limited sensitivity of the grading scale to detect partial improvement. No clear differences in healing or improvement rates were observed between groups. The study does not establish the efficacy of LAIO, with or without sucralfate.

title: National surveillance for African horse sickness in the Republic of Korea, 2020-2025.
abstract: African horse sickness (AHS) is a severe vector-borne disease of equids that may cause substantial mortality and economic losses following introduction into disease-free regions. To assess evidence of African horse sickness virus (AHSV) circulation in the Republic of Korea by integrating national serological surveillance of domestic horses with targeted monitoring of Culicoides biting midges. From 2020 to 2025, 8,681 equine serum samples from 17 regions were tested for AHSV antibodies by blocking enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Culicoides collected at horse facilities were identified morphologically, pooled, and screened for AHSV RNA by real-time reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction. All 8,681 serum samples were seronegative. Among 671 Culicoides specimens from 12 species, C. arakawae predominated (489/671, 72.9%), followed by C. punctatus and C. tainanus (52/671, 7.7% each). Neither AHSV RNA nor the confirmed vectors C. imicola and C. bolitinos were detected. Although the number of Culicoides specimens collected was relatively low, no evidence of AHSV circulation was detected in the sampled horse population or vector collections in the Republic of Korea. Continued integrated serological and vector surveillance is warranted to support early detection and preparedness against the introduction of AHS.

title: Genetic parameters and effects of inbreeding on morphometric and performance traits in a population of Mangalarga Marchador horses.
abstract: Inbreeding in equine populations is concerning because it may affect morphological traits and reduce athletic performance.
